5.0.0.en: "After this": that is, after the miracle of healing the son of the king's servant, Christ went up to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover for the second time. He did not mention the kind of feast, because his focus was on the service of souls and preaching, and the time had not yet come for Him to attend the Passover at which He would offer Himself on the Cross.

5.1.0.en: "The sheep market" [lit. the sheep gate]: the gate of the city nearest to the temple. It was given this name because the sheep for the sacrifice were brought through it.

5.1.1.en: "Bethesda": a pool about one hundred meters in length, and its width ranged between 50 and 70 meters, with rows of columns along its sides dividing it into five waiting courts; these porches were built to receive visitors seeking healing. As for the name "Bethesda," its meaning is: house of mercy, and the sick with every kind of chronic disease used to come to it, to obtain healing whenever the still water was stirred by the action of an angel. And the word "withered" means: stiff in the joints.

5.1.2.en: This miracle shows the difference between the pool of the Old Testament, which is temporary and not permanent, and was for healing bodies by going down into it, and the New Testament, which gives permanent healing of spirit and body, as happens in the sacrament of Baptism.

5.1.3.en: (2) The healing of the sick man of Bethesda (vv. 5-9):

5.1.4.en: 5- "And a certain man was there, which had an infirmity thirty and eight years. 6- When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole? 7- The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me. 8- Jesus saith unto him, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk."

5.1.5.en: 9- "And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath."

5.2.0.en: The purpose of mentioning this miracle is not the healing of the paralytic in itself, but to highlight Christ's surpassing authority. For this reason St. John mentioned the long duration of the illness, and the bitter state of despair through which the sick man was passing, to highlight thereby God's visitation of man with His mercies.

5.2.2.en: (1) That it was Christ who saw him and began the conversation with him, for God is the One who visits and seeks out every soul in weariness or distress, and He forgets no one.

5.2.3.en: (2) Although Christ is the initiator, and He wants salvation for everyone, the grace of salvation also requires man's will for the salvation of his own soul. For this reason Christ asked him this question, which seems strange to a sick man: "Wilt thou be made whole?"

5.2.4.en: (3) God's mercy and His unlimited power, which shatters all despair. Although the sick man had been crippled for 38 years, He commanded him to rise and walk, and he was healed at once.

5.3.0.en: The word "immediately" indicates the power of the miracle and the authority of the Lord Christ over disease. That the man should carry his bed and be able to walk after these long years of lying down is a matter beyond mental conception: that these slackened muscles should suddenly be strengthened, without any supplementary treatments, leaves the observer no room except to say that this is the hand of God.

5.3.1.en: My beloved God, You sought out the sick man lying there, while I am still bound by my sins ... I want to be healed, but the will is weak ... So come, beloved, and speak a word that strengthens my resolve and makes me rise, casting behind me all the years of laziness and weakness, leaving my despair, holding fast to my hope in You.

5.4.0.en: The prophet Jeremiah says: "Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding; which have eyes, and see not" (Jer 5:21)."

5.4.1.en: St. Cyril the Great says that this verse applies to the attitude of the Jews toward this miracle ... They forgot the power of the Healer, and the work of mercy offered by God, and held to the letter of the commandment, empty of the Spirit of God. So it is, beloved, with us also in our stubbornness: often we do not see the good will of God. Would that You, my God, open our eyes and our hearts and our understandings, so that we may understand and see Your works and Your wisdom, and leave our evils and our condemnation of others.

5.5.0.en: It was not the Lord's nature to declare Himself, He who did not receive glory from men.

5.5.1.en: So may we also learn not to boast of what we do before people, learning humility from our God, and not seeking to receive the praise of people, remembering that our Father who sees in secret will reward us openly.

5.6.0.en: The man met Christ again in the temple; and in Christ's new conversation with him we find the following meanings:

5.6.1.en: First: that this illness was the result of a previous sin, for the phrase "sin no more" means "do not sin again," and Christ, by His divinity, knew this sin.

5.6.2.en: Second: man must always remember God's work with him and His kindness, and thank God. And most important, he must not forget and return again to what he had left.

5.6.3.en: Third: that the man who ignores God's repeated mercies exposes himself to a greater punishment, "a worse thing" will come upon him.

5.7.0.en: As for the man's purpose in informing the Jews, it was to clear himself of the charge of carrying the bed, for fear of the Jews and their killing him in carrying out the commandment of the Law. This shows the weakness of this man's faith, for he cared about pleasing the Jews more than holding to Christ's teachings.

5.8.0.en: St. John shows here the extent of the Jews' hatred of the person of Christ, to the point of seeking to kill Him. He attributed this intense hatred to two reasons. The first: breaking the Sabbath, forgetting the great miracle. The second: the manner in which Christ described the relationship with God as that of His Father, but from another angle, different from God's fatherhood of all; Christ stresses the natural fatherhood of the Father to the Son, which is restricted to Him alone, making Himself equal with the Father in essence, and in that their work is one and continuous. For this reason the Jews sought to kill Him on the charge of blasphemy, because they understood Christ's intention perfectly, yet they rejected Him.

5.9.0.en: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work": by this verse Christ makes clear to the Jews that even on the Sabbath the Father works, and does not cease to care for His creation. Consequently the Son, who is one with Him in essence, shares His work. If God is thus, then we also must not cease from serving God and His creation all the days. In this way the Sabbath moves from the letter of the commandment to its spirit and content.

5.10.0.en: In His answer to the Jews the Lord draws us gradually into the depth of theology, making clear this mysterious relationship between the Father and the Son in the one essence ... proving His divinity through: (1) Unity of will: the Son cannot have a will separate in action from the will of His Father, because they are one in essence. (2) Inseparability: although the Word took flesh, through the divine essence He is in constant communion with the Father, seeing and beholding all that He does, for the two are one.

5.10.1.en: (3) Unity of power: in that all that the Father does, the Son does likewise, for He is in no way less than the Father in power, because He is one with Him in will and inseparability.

5.10.2.en: (4) Unity of love: in the Father's opening Himself to the Son with all love, so that the Son knows all the Father's mysteries, works and purposes. This too is evidence of the Son's divinity, who must possess unlimited knowledge and understanding in order to comprehend all God's works and purposes.

5.10.3.en: "Greater works": Christ here foretells the coming and wonderful miracles, some of which will be shown in the coming verses, or which St. John will mention in the following chapters. We note that the Jews marvel, but they do not believe.

5.10.4.en: My beloved God and good Savior ... as You, in the fullness of love, were one with Your good Father in will and inseparability ... we too, Your people, long to submit with all our hearts and our will to Your love and Your voice in our lives. Grant us, Lord, to be one with You, as You asked for us, so that we leave everything that hinders us, and turn toward You and follow You with all our hearts.

5.11.0.en: Another direct proof of Christ's divinity in His heavenly power, equal to the Father's, in raising the dead, which is something no man can do. The phrase "quickeneth whom He will" Christ applied to Himself, distinguishing Himself from some prophets who raised the dead, such as Elijah and Elisha, through their prayers to God. As for the power of Christ, its source is Himself and His divine will alone. And Christ offers another proof of His divinity in that He is the Judge, an attribute restricted to God alone, who knows the deeds of men and the secrets of their hearts.

5.12.0.en: Another proof of Christ's divinity, as He made honoring the Father and honoring the Son one indivisible thing. If the honor of God and honoring Him has no equal honor, and no man approaches it, at the same time Christ declares that honoring the Son is equal to and bound up with honoring the Father; this is another testimony to the Son's equality with the Father in glorification, worship and Godhead.

5.13.0.en: Christ affirms once again the unity between the Son and the Father: in hearing the word of the Son and believing in God the Father. The word of the Son is the commandment of the Father Himself; and without faith in God the Father and obedience to the commandment of God the Son, no one will have eternal life, and none will escape judgment. But whoever does this has passed from spiritual death to life in Christ, by faith, repentance and obeying Christ's commandments.

5.13.1.en: My beloved brother, eternal life has been prepared for you by God out of His great prior love. So come, let us together submit to His commandment, that we may have rest here and eternal life there.

5.14.0.en: "The hour is coming, and now is": the Lord Christ used the word "now" as a preparation for what He will speak of in verse 28, which He did not mention in it. "Now" here means the spiritual resurrection by repentance, for everyone who hears the word of the Son of God, accepts it and acts on it. But the one who refuses repentance, and ignores the call of the Lord Christ, is dead in his sins to eternal destruction. This verse reminds us of what the divine inspiration said in the Old Testament by the mouth of the prophet Isaiah: "In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in the day of salvation have I helped thee" (Isa 49:8). And in the New Testament, divine inspiration affirms that the time of repentance is now, not tomorrow, and allows no postponement, when it said by the mouth of the Apostle Paul: "In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2).

5.14.1.en: If God's mercies have opened their arms to receive you by repentance and confession now, why are you not received, and why do you prefer to remain in death rather than life by responding to Christ's call to you?!

5.15.0.en: This verse is a new proof of Christ's divinity. The attribute of self-existent, uncreated life belongs to God alone, who is its source and giver, and the Son also, because He is God, has this very attribute: First: that He is uncreated.

5.15.1.en: Second: that He has the very authority of the Father in granting this life to whom He wills, for He is its source, as John said before: "In Him was life" (ch. 1:4).

5.16.0.en: That is, the divine Being gave the right of judgment to the Son, just as it is the right of the Father (v. 22), and of the Holy Spirit (ch. 16:8). This is because the divine nature is one in essence, but judgment is given to the Son who, by His incarnation, lived our life and suffered, tempted in all things except sin alone. Divine justice and mercy alone made the incarnate Christ, who became man, the judge of all humanity. He is the Judge on the one hand, and the advocate for man on the other, for He pleads for us by His redemption and judges us innocent.

5.17.0.en: "Marvel not at this": that is, at what He has said before and what He will say after it, for Christ knows the difficulty of accepting what He says for the human mind that is not prepared to deal with divine truths. As for the hour of which the Lord speaks, it is the hour of the Second Coming and judgment, in which all will hear His voice, the righteous and the wicked, going either to eternal life or to eternal destruction ... And we must not miss here, dear reader, the clarity of the verse that recompense and judgment are for the works that man did throughout his life, whether good or evil. And despite the clarity of the verse here, we wonder at those who teach that works have no relation to judgment (compare Mt 25:31-46).

5.17.1.en: O that I might seize, my God, the opportunity of this life to do good as You did (compare Acts 10:38), and not scatter my times here and there.

5.17.2.en: My God ... always put the thought of judgment in my heart, so that my longings for eternity are stirred on the one hand, and I feel that for every moment and every work I will give an account, and so my weak soul is strengthened on the other hand.

5.18.0.en: The Lord Christ here repeats what He said before in (v. 19) about the union of will and work with the Father, so that there can be no separation for a single moment. For this reason, all that He does is the will and the purpose of the Father Himself. This confirms the complete agreement between them, and the meaning of "I can do nothing" here is: "I do not will," as we say: "God cannot lie" ...

5.18.1.en: And the expression "as I hear" is also similar to what came in (v. 19), that the Son does what the Father does, and it affirms the same previous meaning, which is the unity of communion between the Father and the Son.

5.18.3.en: 31- "If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. 32- There is another that beareth witness of me; and I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true. 33- Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth. 34- But I receive not testimony from man: but these things I say, that ye might be saved. 35- He was a burning and a shining light: and ye were willing for a season to rejoice in his light. 36- But I have greater witness than that of John: for the works which the Father hath given me to finish, the same works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father hath sent me. 37- And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape. 38- And ye have not his word abiding in you: for whom he hath sent, him ye believe not. 39- Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. 40- And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life."

5.19.0.en: These verses speak of the witness of the Father to the Son, and of the witness of John the Baptist also.

5.19.1.en: And Christ declared the purpose of this witness: He is not in need of it, but He mentions it for the salvation of the Jews themselves (v. 34).

5.20.0.en: Christ begins His speech here knowing what was in the minds of the Jews and in their Law, and in general custom and the Law, that a man's witness to himself is not accepted, as a preparation for presenting the greatest Witness, who is God the Father Himself (the other witness). It is known that the strength and value of a testimony derive from the standing of the witness, so Christ offered the witness of the Father, which allows no room for doubt or refutation, although if He were to bear witness of Himself, His witness is true (ch. 8:14).

5.21.0.en: Christ moves here to the witness of John, who is a second witness with standing among the Jews, indeed it was they who went to him to question him, and his witness came declaring that Christ is the truth. As for Christ's not receiving the Baptist's witness, this does not mean rejecting it, but is a hidden allusion to His divinity. For despite the greatness of the witness, it is unacceptable that God's truthfulness should depend on the witness of a man. But the Lord adds the Baptist's witness to the Father's witness so that the Jews may believe, for faith in the person of Christ is the first condition of salvation, and Christ wants nothing but the salvation of His people.

5.22.0.en: A second witness that Christ gives to the Baptist, that he was the shining lamp, after He had described him as the greatest of those born of women, and this is an incidental verse in the context of the speech. But Christ said it for two reasons. The first: that He gives every man his due and forgets no one's labor. The second: that He rebukes the Jews who gathered around the Baptist for a season, a short period of 6 months, and after his imprisonment returned to their former conduct, without the influence of the Baptist's words continuing in their lives.

5.22.1.en: My God and my Lord, the Baptist was faithful in his mission, a witness and a martyr for the divine truth, and his praise came from Your holy mouth ... Give me, my God, the spirit of the Baptist and some of his strength, so that I too may bear witness to You by my works, as he did by his words and deeds, and so be a shining lamp, a light to the world, that I may fulfill Your good will in my life.

5.23.0.en: A third witness that the Lord Christ gives, greater than the witness of any man, and more certain, namely those miraculous works, such as the healing of the sick, the opening of the eyes of the blind, and the raising of the dead, works that none before Him had matched in power, greatness, number and variety, so as to bear witness to His divinity. As for the expression "the Father hath given me to finish," its meaning is that the Son carries out the will of the Father, as it came in (ch. 1:18): "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him," and Christ also adds that He is the Father's voice and shape.

5.24.0.en: The witness of the Father Himself, which He gave to the Son through the prophecies of the Old Testament and the types of the Law, which are the words of the Father that represent His voice and shape. But despite this, the Jews went astray; and instead of accepting eternal life, they rejected it by their rejection of Christ Himself.

5.25.0.en: If Christ had earlier refused the witness of men to Him, and offered other witnesses not subject to human standards or measures, He also refuses to receive the glory offered to Him by men, but wants to draw them to faith in Him, and consequently to the salvation of their souls.

5.26.0.en: The first reason for the Jews' not accepting Christ is the absence of the love of God from their hearts, without which man cannot recognize the Son. The proof that they did not love God is that He came in His Father's name, whom they claim to love, and they did not receive Him. But if another came in his own name, and the allusion here is to the false messiahs who appeared from time to time, presenting themselves and seeking honor for themselves, the Jews would receive them; so Christ here wonders at their conduct.

5.27.0.en: The second reason for not accepting Christ is the Jews' deviation, and their desire for worldly glory instead of the glory that God gives to His children in their humility, for the sin of boasting and seeking vain glory from men turns man's heart away from God so that he does not accept Him, but is content to remain confined within himself. The truth is therefore clear: either man seeks his own glory at the expense of God's glory, or he seeks God's glory at the expense of himself.

5.27.1.en: My God and Savior ... You humbled Yourself, and did not seek Your own glory, though You are all glory. And I, wretched, am still looking for praise here and there. Help me, my God, to rebuke this accursed self that stands in the way of enjoying Your perfect love, and growing in knowing You, and knowing all Your mysteries.

5.28.0.en: He whom you suppose to be an intercessor and mediator for you, the prophet Moses, is himself the one who accuses you before God. For all that Moses wrote had Christ as its goal. The Jews' unbelief in Christ means rejecting the Law that Moses wrote. If they do not believe the words of the greatest of their prophets, how then will they believe in Christ?!

5.28.1.en: The feeding of the multitudes; walking on the water; the sacrament of Communion of the Body and Blood of Christ
